A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CREME framework and four optimization applications despite the changed title. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support comparison; relocated proofs and experiments can be matched.

before.justification: Section 4 and Appendix D report original synthetic experiments evaluating validity, accuracy, and robustness selection across four optimization problems.

after.justification: Section 4 and Appendix F report original experiments, including updated estimator comparisons, post-selection recalibration results, and new sensitivity and runtime measurements.

M1.justification: V1 constructs and returns a frontier using one calibration dataset. V2's Algorithm 1 and Section 3.3 introduce random splitting, selection using the first subset's frontier, and risk recalibration using the second subset. This substantially changes the procedure and output, although the underlying risk-estimator formulas remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same synthetic linear programming, newsvendor, portfolio selection, and shortest-path tasks. The distributions, optimization formulations, and degenerate-context setting in v1 Appendix D.1 are retained in v2 Appendix F.1. No new dataset or task domain is evaluated.

E2.justification: Monte Carlo remains the comparison method for validity–accuracy evaluation. Parametric quantile, empirical quantile, and conformal prediction remain the three decision-quality baselines. The added post-hoc curves represent the proposed CREME extension rather than an additional baseline.

E3.justification: V2 evaluates the new split-calibration procedure alongside the original estimator and adds a grid of n and |Λ| values in {10, 20, 30}, measuring frontier gap and runtime. The existing sample-size sweep and decision-quality settings are retained. The split proportions and allocation of experimental sample budgets are not specified.

E4.justification: New Section 4.3 and Table 1 examine how calibration sample size and robustness-grid size affect approximation error and computational cost. This extends sensitivity analysis within the retained tasks. The existing robustness-parameter and preference-weight analyses in Figures 6–7 remain unchanged.

E5.justification: Table 1 introduces explicit mean ± standard deviation reporting over 20 trials. Both versions already report averaging the main evaluations over 20 independent trials and smoothing estimators over 10 replications; an increase in repeated-run counts is not established.

E6.justification: Figures 3–4 contain updated curves and additional post-hoc results, with v2 reporting greater conservativeness and a validity–accuracy trade-off. Table 1 adds numerical gap and runtime results; for example, linear programming at n=30 and |Λ|=30 has gap 0.06±0.02 and runtime 2.98±0.13 seconds. These are newly reported results, not demonstrated same-setting gains over v1. Appendix Figures 6–7 are retained.

T1.justification: V2 adds Corollary 3.9, defining a selection-dependent validity-degradation term, its proof in Appendix E, and a conditional-exchangeability argument for split-data recalibration in Remark E.1. The original fixed-parameter validity, finite-sample error bound, Pareto results, and illustrative counterexample are substantially retained and reorganized.

C1.justification: The three central contributions concerning inverse CRC, certified risk frontiers, and robustness calibration remain. V2's introduction explicitly adds post-selection recalibration to the guarantee narrative. Its abstract also removes the claims of being the first principled methodology and having sharper performance than existing approaches.

C2.justification: Section 3.3 newly explains why choosing robustness from the calibration frontier can invalidate fixed-parameter guarantees and motivates independent recalibration. V2 also interprets the added post-hoc conservativeness and runtime results. Its conclusion replaces the scalability-focused limitation with explicit emphasis on requiring a bounded loss supremum.

D1.justification: V2 adds measured execution times and associated configuration information in Section 4.3 and Table 1. The Python, CVXPY, cvxpylayers, default solver settings, and heuristic loss-bound estimation from 100 simulations remain documented. Neither version provides a concrete code-access link; v2 also leaves split proportions unspecified.

R1.justification: Related work is substantially expanded to cover multidimensional conformal-set geometry, additional CRC extensions, and post-selection inference, including Johnstone and Cox, Cohen et al., and Hegazy et al. Positioning shifts from avoiding adaptivity penalties and claiming sharper bounds than e-value approaches toward diagnostic auditing and established data-splitting strategies.

P1.justification: V2 changes the title, extensively rewrites related work and experimental discussion, and reorganizes the theoretical exposition and appendices. The original main-text validity proof moves to Appendix A, the illustrative examples move from A to C, and experimental details move from D to F. These changes substantially alter the narrative structure.

P2.justification: V2 changes the document template, typography, headers, author block, and page layout. Figures 3–4 are redrawn with additional green post-hoc series, revised legends and scales; Table 1 is added and Algorithm 1 is expanded and relocated. The graphics in Figures 1–2 and 5–7 are retained.

improvement.justification: The selection-bias analysis and holdout argument address an important gap between v1's fixed-parameter guarantees and adaptive robustness selection. However, v2's Algorithm 1 divides subset loss sums by total n, whereas Appendix E requires subset-size normalization. Table 1 also repeats every entry for |Λ|=10 and 20, leaving that sensitivity evidence unclear. These unresolved inconsistencies limit confidence in the main addition and prevent a reliable net quality judgment.
